cues.text: A Belgian Immigrant's Vow
Born in Belgium in 1831, Adele Brise immigrated with her family to the frontier woods of northeastern Wisconsin in 1855, settling near what is now Champion.
As a girl in Belgium, Adele and several friends had privately vowed to devote their lives to God's service.
Poor eyesight kept her from the convent she had hoped to enter, and she carried that unfulfilled vow across the ocean into pioneer farm life's hardships.

We recognize in this early disappointment something the Lord so often permits before a greater calling: a door closed in one direction so that a very different door, still unimagined, might open in its place.
A Lady Between Two Trees
In early October 1859, the twenty-eight-year-old Adele carried wheat to a distant gristmill along a forest path.
There, she saw a woman clothed in dazzling white standing silently between a maple and a hemlock tree, a crown of stars above flowing golden hair.

Frightened, she said nothing until the vision reappeared several days later as she walked the same path to Sunday Mass, this time accompanied by her sister and a neighbor — though only Adele could see the figure standing there.
"Gather the Children"
On this second encounter, the Lady finally spoke, identifying herself as the Queen of Heaven and giving Adele a specific and demanding commission.
She was to gather the children of this wild frontier country and teach them what they needed to know for salvation.
So many, scattered across the wilderness with few priests or schools to reach them, were growing up in real ignorance of the faith.

Adele accepted the charge without hesitation, and from that day forward devoted herself entirely to walking from farm to farm, often fifty miles in a stretch, teaching catechism to any family willing to receive her.
Opposition and Perseverance
Adele's mission drew both admiration and real resistance.

Church authorities did not formally approve the reported visions during Adele's lifetime, and the question of their authenticity remained unresolved until the diocesan investigation that preceded the 2010 declaration.
Her small, informal community of lay women faced years of institutional suspicion while building a chapel, and later a school, on the apparition's very site.
Adele bore this opposition, as she had borne the vision itself, with the same steady, unglamorous persistence, never abandoning either her teaching or her devotion to the chapel she had helped raise.

Adele herself never wavered under this scrutiny, continuing her walking mission through Wisconsin winters and summers alike for nearly four decades, teaching hundreds of frontier children the catechism they might otherwise never have received at all.
Spared from the Peshtigo Fire

The community's faith in the site was tested dramatically in October 1871, when the catastrophic Peshtigo Fire — still the deadliest wildfire in American history — swept through the surrounding region, destroying nearly everything in its path.
Adele and those sheltering at her chapel processed through the night around its grounds, carrying a statue of Our Lady and praying without ceasing.
When dawn came, the fire had stopped at the property's very fence line, sparing the chapel and everyone within it.
The land all around lay burned to ash.
Witnesses who sheltered at the chapel that night recalled the surrounding forest and farmland burning to the ground.
Not a single ember crossed onto the property itself, a boundary so precise that neighboring families credited it to nothing less than the Virgin's own direct protection.
Legacy
Adele continued her teaching mission until her death in 1896, and the small community and school she founded grew, over the following century and a half, into a shrine of quiet but steady devotion.
On December 8, 2010, Bishop David Ricken of Green Bay formally declared the 1859 apparitions to Adele Brise "worthy of belief."
This was the first Marian apparition ever to receive full diocesan approval on American soil.
The National Shrine of Our Lady of Good Help remains, to this day, the only site in the United States built upon a Church-approved appearance of the Blessed Virgin.
It is a wooded Wisconsin path transformed by one immigrant woman's vow into hallowed ground.
